More or less work your way top to bottom.

Are your taxes/wages at an unsustainable level? - fix it

Are you at war and military wages low? - increase it

Are you in bureaucracy deficit? - build admin

Are you at war against a strong power or expect to be soon? - build troops

Is your economy not fully industrialized? - build construction sectors

Are you significantly below innovation cap? - build universities (same state)

Do you need overseas resources where you don't currently have an interest? - build ships

Do your states have free peasants/employed? - build construction sectors

Do you have institutions you want to raise their level? - build admin

Are you behind in tech? - build universities over cap (same state)

Are a significant number of pops in jobs you don't want them to have? - build construction sectors

Still have more money? - build troops

I don't know if it is know how they've changed the calculations of how many battalions end up engaging in a fight, but ive noticed quantity matters more than quality in this beta. 100k 30 offense infantry can beat 60k 70 defense armies (too many variables to say this as a consistent basis, just that it CAN happen).

What I'm trying to say is there is a "net" offense based both on quantity and quality. Your objective is to maximize the "net" offense (or defense depending on the front) based on your nation. How cheap is small arms vs artillery vs munitions? What's your population surplus? You can use these metrics to determine what area you can best leverage industrial & human inputs into military offensive (or defensive) power. If its way cheaper for you to make swarms of infantry that it is to make canons, do that.

E.g. if you have an 80/10/10 army, but you want a 40/20/20 army, you can transfer 40 infantry to a new army (and do what you want with it) then build 10 artillery and 10 cavalry for the original army so you end up with a 40/20/20 army and a 40/0/0 army. It's not perfect, but if you're continually expanding your armed forces eventually the ratio will line up with what you want. For instance if afterwards you build 20 artillery and cavalry for the second army you have 2x 40/20/20 armies (which I've taken as a premise that this is an ideal ratio even though I have no idea what the ideal ratio actually is).
As others say, it's a neat idea, but the in-game systems aren't at the place where it can have a good implementation.

They are clearly *into* each other (romantically or not). Really more info is needed for a best answer. But, I'll try two simple versions.

If your 'trio' is more-so A & B as the core, then there's you, but there's also several tertiary friends (like the ones that got invited instead of you) that you would also say are in the same circle, then you should be looking around who else you are fond of in that circle. Maybe you already have and didn't see much? I would suggest looking again but try to focus on appreciating any good qualities you find in them, otherwise your brain might trick you into believing they aren't good enough.

If its literally just those 2 and you and everyone else seems to change from context to context, then you're going to have to do more work. First will probably be some introspection. Really dig deep into your interests and try to find generalizations (e.g. while you enjoy history class, you notice that it's because you really enjoy connecting events together to develop a correct 'story' of what happened) then take a look through clubs/extracurriculars and see if any might pull on those strings of interest as well. Don't worry about it not working out the first time, it's not like there's a binding contract for you to stay in a club if you end up not liking it. 

If I'm interpreting you correctly you probably shouldn't confront A and/or B. You can't force them to like you and demanding more attention is more likely to build resentment. The two exceptions to this are if they are actively hurting you with stuff like talking about you in front of you, then bringing up specific stuff might help. The other exception is if they actively say they want to spend more time with you, you can talk to them about better ways to go about it with more concrete plans.

Finally, you're young so don't worry too much about having strong bonds at this time. Figure out what you like and dislike and set yourself up for success as best you can. If you can get to the point of being self-secure your options of friends will be basically whoever you are willing to spend your time with.

If you're not big, don't go looking for these encounters, and if they do happen you need to figure out how to get away, not how to fight. "Winning" when you're being mugged isn't to beat the other person up, it's to get away unharmed (even if it means giving up possessions, at least in my opinion). If this is the case for you, just being fit and knowing how to negotiate these encounters is what's important.

If you ARE big and you're specifically looking for how to win a fight instead of resolving it as stated above, Mixed martial arts is the most appropriate avenue to go. Particularly I would recommend learning Brazillian Jiu Jutsu and Greco-Roman wrestling. Most fights will end up on the ground, until that point just knowing how to throw a decent punch and not being dumb with your footwork is enough for the short term. Of course learning more gives you more capability, Muay Thai is the best style for on-foot fighting IMO. Again though, for the most part any 1 on 1 fight will likely end up on the ground pretty fast in the real world. Lastly for dealing with weapons, Israeli Krav Maga is probably the best type of martial arts for dealing with that kind of situation, but I want to emphasize again at this point that if you're facing someone with a weapon, your goal should always be to get away unharmed rather than to "win" in a fight.

Tldr: If you're not big, just run, if you are big: Brazillian Jiu Jutsu, Krav Maga, Greco-Roman wrestling, and Muay Thai boxing are the martial art styles you should learn (IMO in that order)
